cards.title: CPR & Defibrillator (AED) Awareness
cards.body:
By the end of this session you can:
- recognise a cardiac arrest
- call 999, send for an AED and start CPR
- use an AED, even without training

cards.title: Heart suddenly stops
cards.body:
A cardiac arrest is when someone's heart suddenly stops and they become unresponsive and are not breathing normally. It can happen to anyone, at any age.

For every minute without CPR and a defibrillator, the chance of survival falls by around 10%.

items.label: Survival lost for every minute without CPR and an AED

cards.title: Call, fetch, start
cards.body: If you find someone collapsed and not breathing normally:

items.title: Send for the AED
items.text: Ask someone to fetch the nearest one

cards.title: How to do compressions
cards.body: Push hard and fast in the centre of the chest.

items.label: Pushes a minute, about the beat of "Stayin' Alive"
Two rescue breaths after every 30 compressions, if trained

cards.title: Hands-only CPR is fine
cards.body:
If you are not trained to give breaths, hands-only CPR is fine and still saves lives.

> Do not worry about doing it perfectly. Doing something is far better than doing nothing.

cards.title: Anyone can use one
cards.body: A defibrillator is designed for anyone to use. You do not need training. Switch it on and it talks you through everything.

items.title: Attach the pads
items.text: To the bare chest, as shown

items.title: It checks the heart
items.text: And tells you if a shock is needed

items.title: Stand clear
items.text: Nobody touching the person at the shock

cards.title: Remember
cards.body:
- Unresponsive and not breathing normally: call 999 and send for the AED
- Push hard and fast in the centre of the chest, 100 to 120 a minute
- Hands-only CPR is fine if you are not trained
- Anyone can use an AED; nobody touches the person at a shock
- Keep going until the emergency services take over

cards.q: In cardiac arrest, the person is unresponsive and not breathing normally.
cards.why: A cardiac arrest is when the heart suddenly stops and the person becomes unresponsive and is not breathing normally.

cards.q: What is the first thing to do when you find someone in cardiac arrest?
options: Make them comfortable and wait for a manager
Give them a drink of water to revive them
Wait and watch for a few minutes
cards.why: Call 999 immediately, put it on speaker, and send someone to fetch the nearest AED.

cards.q: Chest compressions should be at a rate of about:
cards.why: Push at 100 to 120 a minute; the beat of "Stayin' Alive" is about right.

cards.q: Hands-only CPR (no breaths) still saves lives if you are not trained.
cards.why: If you are not trained, hands-only CPR is fine and still saves lives.

cards.q: Do you need special training to use a defibrillator (AED)?
options: No, it talks you through it
Yes, a manager must authorise it
cards.why: An AED is designed for anyone to use: switch it on and it talks you through everything.

cards.q: Nobody should be touching the person when the AED delivers a shock.
cards.why: Make sure nobody is touching the person when it delivers a shock.

cards.q: Roughly how much does survival fall for each minute without CPR and a defibrillator?
cards.why: For every minute without CPR and a defibrillator, the chance of survival falls by around 10%.

cards.q: Where on the body do you push for chest compressions?
options: The left side of the chest
cards.why: Push hard and fast in the centre of the chest.

cards.q: You should continue CPR until the emergency services take over or the person shows signs of life.
cards.why: Keep going with CPR and the AED until help arrives and takes over, or the person shows signs of life.

options: Something only first aiders may do
Likely to hurt them more than help
cards.why: Do not worry about doing it perfectly: doing something is far better than doing nothing.
